message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"12.11","text":"But Peter, on hearing this, wept out of sympathy and immediately said to his genuine companions, “If anyone had suffered these things while living in reverence for God—the kinds of things this man’s father has suffered—he would immediately have attached the cause to the teaching of reverence for God, naming the evil one as responsible. So too it happens that the wretched nations suffer, and we who revere God are unaware of it. I have rightly called them wretched, because they wander here and do not obtain the hope there. For those who suffer distressing things while living in reverence for God suffer them as payment exacted for transgressions.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ὑπὸ συμπαθείας ἐδάκρυσεν","chosen":"wept out of sympathy","rationale":"Preserves συμπάθεια as compassionate fellow-feeling rather than merely sadness."},{"source_quote":"τοῖς συνοῦσιν γνησίοις","chosen":"his genuine companions","rationale":"γνήσιοι characterizes those accompanying Peter as genuine or faithful; “genuine” retains the explicit adjective."},{"source_quote":"τῷ τῆς θεοσεβείας λόγῳ τὴν αἰτίαν προσῆπτεν","chosen":"attached the cause to the teaching of reverence for God","rationale":"λόγος may mean teaching, account, or rationale; “teaching” fits the religious context, while the construction depicts attaching the cause to it."},{"source_quote":"ἐπιγράφων τὸν πονηρόν","chosen":"naming the evil one as responsible","rationale":"ἐπιγράφω can mean inscribe, designate, or attribute; here it identifies the evil one as responsible."},{"source_quote":"τοῖς ταλαιπώροις ἔθνεσιν","chosen":"the wretched nations","rationale":"ἔθνη may mean nations, peoples, or, in a religious contrast, Gentiles. “Nations” preserves the broader wording without excluding the contextual sense “Gentiles.”"},{"source_quote":"ἐνταῦθα ἁλῶνται","chosen":"they wander here","rationale":"ἁλῶνται is understood as the contracted present form of ἀλάομαι, “wander.” Contextually this may imply straying or wandering in error, but it does not denote being caught or convicted."},{"source_quote":"εἰς ἔκπραξιν παραπτωμάτων","chosen":"as payment exacted for transgressions","rationale":"ἔκπραξις denotes exaction or collection of what is due, here presenting suffering as payment associated with transgressions."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ἐν. θεοσεβείᾳ","issue":"The verified print places a full stop inside the prepositional phrase. The surviving words support reading ἐν with θεοσεβείᾳ continuously; treating the stop as intrusive editorial or printing punctuation is provisional but requires no missing text.","proposed_reading":"ἐν θεοσεβείᾳ","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"ἐνταῦθα ἁλῶνται","issue":"The verified printed form has rough breathing. It is interpreted as the contracted present of ἀλάομαι, “wander,” without altering the supplied spelling; the breathing is treated as a disclosed orthographic feature, not evidence for a capture-related verb.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"12.12","text":"After Peter had said this, one of our company dared to speak for everyone and urged him to sail earlier the next morning to Aradus, the island opposite, which I think was not even a full thirty stadia away, to view the two vinewood columns there, which were of enormous thickness. Peter, being accommodating, agreed and said, “When you disembark from the ship, do not go in all at once as a large group to see the things you desire. I do not want the citizens turning toward us.” So we sailed and, in a fraction of an hour, put in at the island. After getting out of the boat, we went in to where the vinewood columns stood; and at the same time, together with them, one person viewed one of Phidias’s works and another a different one.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"εἷς τις τῶν ἐν ἡμῖν τολμήσας ἀντὶ πάντων","chosen":"one of our company dared to speak for everyone","rationale":"The act supplied by τολμήσας is implicit; speaking is supported by the following request, while ἀντὶ πάντων means on behalf of all."},{"source_quote":"ὡς ἐπὶ ἱστορίᾳ","chosen":"to view","rationale":"ἱστορία here denotes inspection or sightseeing, not the writing of history."},{"source_quote":"τῶν ἐκεῖ ἀμπελίων δύο στύλων","chosen":"the two vinewood columns there","rationale":"ἀμπέλινος describes something made from or associated with a vine; “vinewood” preserves the material image."},{"source_quote":"οὐ γὰρ βούλομαι στρέμματα γίνεσθαι εἰς ἡμᾶς τῶν πολιτῶν","chosen":"I do not want the citizens turning toward us","rationale":"The source-transparent wording treats στρέμματα as turnings directed toward the visitors. In context this may mean attracting the citizens’ attention or causing them to turn and look; “the citizens turning against us,” implying hostility or disturbance, is also possible but is not required by the noun itself."},{"source_quote":"ῥοπῇ ὥρας","chosen":"in a fraction of an hour","rationale":"ῥοπή can denote a brief turn or moment; the phrase indicates a short portion of an hour, with “in a moment” also possible."},{"source_quote":"ὁμῶς ἅμα αὐτοῖς ἄλλος ἄλλο τι τῶν Φειδίου ἔργων ἐθεώρει","chosen":"at the same time, together with them, one person viewed one of Phidias’s works and another a different one","rationale":"The distributive ἄλλος ἄλλο τι is explicit. The referent of αὐτοῖς may be the columns or other members of the party, so the English pronoun preserves that ambiguity."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"12.13","text":"Peter alone did not consider it necessary to go and view the sights there. But after watching closely for some time a woman who was sitting outside, in front of the doors, and begging for food, he said, “Woman, what limb are you missing, that you have submitted yourself to so great an indignity—I mean begging—instead of working with the hands God has given you to obtain your daily food?” She groaned and replied, “If only I had hands capable of working! But now they retain only the form of hands, since they are dead, tortured by my own bites.” Peter asked, “What is the cause of your having suffered this terrible thing?” She answered, “Weakness of soul, and nothing more. For if I had possessed a courageous resolve, a cliff was there, and so was the deep; from there I could have thrown myself and gained relief from the evils that cause me pain.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἐπὶ τὴν τῶν ἐκεῖ ἱστορίαν γενέσθαι","chosen":"to go and view the sights there","rationale":"ἱστορία again denotes personal observation or sightseeing, and γενέσθαι with ἐπί conveys going for that purpose."},{"source_quote":"πυκνὰ κατανοήσας","chosen":"after watching closely for some time","rationale":"πυκνά can indicate repeated or sustained attention, while κατανοέω denotes attentive observation."},{"source_quote":"τοσαύτην ὕβριν ἀνεδέξω","chosen":"you have submitted yourself to so great an indignity","rationale":"ὕβρις here denotes degrading treatment or humiliation rather than merely pride; ἀναδέχομαι presents her as taking it upon herself."},{"source_quote":"χεῖρες ὑπουργεῖν δυνάμεναι","chosen":"hands capable of working","rationale":"ὑπουργεῖν literally means to serve or render assistance; in context it means functioning for useful work."},{"source_quote":"ὑπὸ δηγμάτων ἐμῶν βεβασανισμέναι","chosen":"tortured by my own bites","rationale":"The possessive ἐμῶν identifies the bites as hers, preserving the image of self-inflicted biting."},{"source_quote":"Ψυχῆς ἀσθένεια","chosen":"Weakness of soul","rationale":"ψυχή may denote soul, life, or inner self; “soul” retains the author’s psychological and moral terminology."},{"source_quote":"ἦν κρημνός, ἦν βυθός","chosen":"a cliff was there, and so was the deep","rationale":"The repeated imperfect ἦν presents the available means of death. A counterfactual English alternative would be “there would have been a cliff and the deep.”"}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"12.14","text":"Peter said, “What then do you think, woman? That those who kill themselves are invariably released from punishment? Or are the souls of those who die in this way not punished in Hades with a worse punishment for their suicide?” She said, “If only I were convinced that souls really are found alive in Hades! Then I would gladly die, despising the punishment, so that I might see my dearly missed ones, even for a single hour.” Peter said, “I wanted to learn what it is that grieves you, woman. For if you tell me, in return for this favor I will fully assure you that souls live in Hades, and instead of a cliff or the deep I will give you a drug, so that, without torment, you may be able to exchange your way of life for living.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"πάντως οἱ ἀναιροῦντες ἑαυτοὺς κολάσεως ἀπαλλάσσονται","chosen":"those who kill themselves are invariably released from punishment","rationale":"πάντως supplies the categorical force, while ἀναιροῦντες ἑαυτούς explicitly refers to taking one’s own life."},{"source_quote":"ἢ μὴ τῇ χείρονι κολάσει","chosen":"Or are ... not punished ... with a worse punishment","rationale":"The negative μή is retained in the rhetorical alternative rather than being smoothed away, although the resulting English question is marked."},{"source_quote":"καὶ ἠγάπων τῆς κολάσεως καταφρονήσασα θανεῖν","chosen":"Then I would gladly die, despising the punishment","rationale":"ἀγαπάω with an infinitive can express being pleased or willing to do something; “gladly” conveys that idiomatic force."},{"source_quote":"τοὺς ἐμοὺς περιποθήτους","chosen":"my dearly missed ones","rationale":"περιπόθητος describes people intensely longed for; “dearly missed” leaves their precise relationship unstated."},{"source_quote":"πληροφορήσω σε","chosen":"I will fully assure you","rationale":"πληροφορέω here means to bring someone to full assurance or conviction."},{"source_quote":"φάρμακον","chosen":"a drug","rationale":"φάρμακον can mean a medicine, remedy, or poison. “Drug” preserves the ambiguity essential to the woman’s subsequent misunderstanding."},{"source_quote":"ὅπως ἀβασανίστως τοῦ ζῆν τὸν βίον μεταλλάξαι δυνηθῇς","chosen":"so that, without torment, you may be able to exchange your way of life for living","rationale":"The main rendering takes τὸν βίον as the object of μεταλλάξαι and τοῦ ζῆν as the genitive counterpart in an exchange: her present way or course of life is exchanged for living. This fits Peter’s offer of a remedy while preserving the wording that the next section calls ambiguous. Alternatively, τὸν βίον may function within ζῆν τὸν βίον, “to live one’s life,” while τοῦ ζῆν marks what she departs from, yielding “depart from living your life.” Another possible attachment takes τοῦ ζῆν attributively or epexegetically with τὸν βίον, yielding “exchange the life you are living.” The construction therefore permits both continued-life and death-oriented understandings; the main rendering is contextual, not asserted as unique."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"12.15","text":"The woman, not understanding what had been said ambiguously, was delighted by the promise and began to speak as follows: “As for my lineage and homeland, I do not think anyone could ever persuade me to disclose them. But what difference does it make to you whether you learn that or only the reason why, in my anguish, I deadened my own hands by biting them? Nevertheless, I will relate my own affairs as far as it is possible for you to hear them. I was of very noble birth, and at the command of a certain ruler I became the wife of a man related to him by blood. After having twin children, I had another son. But my husband’s brother went mad and fell no less deeply in love with me, unfortunate as I was and deeply devoted to chastity. Since I wanted neither to consent to my would-be lover nor to disclose to my husband his brother’s desire for me, I formed a plan so that I would neither defile myself by committing adultery, nor violate my husband’s bed, nor make brother an enemy to brother, nor subject the entire family, a prominent one, to everyone’s reproach. As I said, I resolved to leave the city with my twin children for a time, until the vile passion of the man who was flattering me in order to dishonor me should also cease. I did, however, leave my other son with his father as a consolation.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τὸ ἀμφιβόλως ῥηθὲν","chosen":"what had been said ambiguously","rationale":"ἀμφιβόλως explicitly identifies Peter’s preceding statement as having a double or uncertain sense."},{"source_quote":"Γένος μὲν καὶ πατρίδα εἰπεῖν οὐκ οἶμαι πεῖσαί ποτε δυνηθῆναί τινα","chosen":"As for my lineage and homeland, I do not think anyone could ever persuade me to disclose them","rationale":"The main rendering takes τινα as the subject of δυνηθῆναι and supplies the woman as the understood object of πεῖσαι, favoring reluctance to disclose in light of her following question. Alternatively, τινα may be the object of πεῖσαι and the woman the understood subject of δυνηθῆναι: “As for stating my lineage and homeland, I do not think I could ever convince anyone.” That reading emphasizes anticipated disbelief, possibly because her present condition contrasts with her claimed noble birth."},{"source_quote":"ὀδυνωμένη δήγμασιν τὰς ἐμὰς ἐνέκρωσα χεῖρας","chosen":"in my anguish, I deadened my own hands by biting them","rationale":"δήγμασιν is taken instrumentally with ἐνέκρωσα, while ὀδυνωμένη describes her anguished condition."},{"source_quote":"ὡς δυνατὸν ἀκοῦσαί σε","chosen":"as far as it is possible for you to hear them","rationale":"The wording limits how much of her circumstances she will disclose; “as much as you are able to hear” is another possible rendering."},{"source_quote":"ἀνδρὶ πρὸς γένους αὐτῷ ὑπάρχοντι","chosen":"a man related to him by blood","rationale":"πρὸς γένους indicates kinship, and αὐτῷ most naturally refers to the ruler."},{"source_quote":"οὐχ ἔλαττον ἠράσθη μου","chosen":"fell no less deeply in love with me","rationale":"The Greek retains a negative comparison without stating its standard. The English preserves “no less” rather than replacing the litotes entirely with a positive intensifier."},{"source_quote":"σφόδρα σωφρονεῖν ἀγαπώσης","chosen":"deeply devoted to chastity","rationale":"σωφρονεῖν here concerns sexual restraint and honorable conduct, while ἀγαπάω expresses her strong commitment to it."},{"source_quote":"μήτε τῷ ἐραστῇ συνθέσθαι","chosen":"neither to consent to my would-be lover","rationale":"συντίθεμαι means agree or consent; “would-be lover” makes clear that his desire had not been accepted."},{"source_quote":"μήτε τῷ ἐμῷ ἀνδρὶ ἀναθέσθαι","chosen":"nor to disclose to my husband","rationale":"ἀνατίθημι can mean refer, report, or entrust a matter to someone; “disclose” fits the concealed proposition."},{"source_quote":"τοῦ ἐπὶ τῇ ἐμῇ ὕβρει κολακεύοντός με","chosen":"of the man who was flattering me in order to dishonor me","rationale":"ὕβρις may imply dishonor, outrage, or sexual violation. “Dishonor” is contextually defensible while leaving the more forceful alternatives disclosed."},{"source_quote":"εἰς παραμυθίαν","chosen":"as a consolation","rationale":"παραμυθία denotes comfort or consolation, explaining why one son remained with his father."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"μὴ · συνεῖσα","issue":"The verified print places a raised dot between the negative μή and the participle it governs. Reading the words continuously yields a defensible construction; treating the dot as intrusive editorial or printing punctuation is provisional and does not imply missing text.","proposed_reading":"μὴ συνεῖσα","blocks_publication":false}]}]}
